justification:
Both round-1 findings are independently re-verified and both hold up as genuine fixes, not just addressed-on-paper.

1) Citation accuracy (was major, now resolved). I fetched https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/BF01386390 myself rather than trusting the writer's claim: CrossRef gives 'Page Numbers: 269-271' for 'A note on two problems in connexion with graphs,' Numerische Mathematik vol. 1 (1959) -- three pages, matching the article's revised text exactly ('in three pages, as one of two short results in the same note ... pp. 269-271'). I also independently checked the new clause the fix added ('one of two short results in the same note') against Wikipedia's Dijkstra's-algorithm history section, which confirms the same 1959 note also contains Dijkstra's rediscovery of Prim's minimum-spanning-tree algorithm -- consistent with the paper's own title ('two problems in connexion with graphs'). The fix did not just patch the flagged number; it is accurate on the claim it added along the way. This closes the major issue cleanly.

2) Exercise framing (was minor, now resolved on independent judgment, not deference to the writer). Re-reading 'Find what makes this Dijkstra slower, not wrong' with the round-1 concern in mind: the added lead-in ('The output above isn't the puzzle: matching the lazy version's distances exactly is what correct removal-before-insert is supposed to do, and it's shown here only so you're not asked to take that on faith. The actual question is about cost, not correctness.') sits directly before the question and names, in plain terms, both what the output block is (a correctness premise) and what it is not (the thing to guess). Judging this independently against the pilot rule's intent -- protecting a reader from having a predict-the-output answer handed to them before they attempt it -- this exercise was never actually predict-the-output: the question never asks the reader to guess a value, only to diagnose why an already-shown-correct approach is worse. The writer's choice to keep the output in place rather than move it is defensible on its own terms (a find-the-bug/cost-analysis exercise legitimately needs the reader to trust the numbers are right before reasoning about why the approach that produced them is expensive), and the new framing sentence removes the 'could momentarily look like guess-the-numbers' ambiguity that was the actual, narrower complaint. I don't see a residual leak here.

Fresh full read beyond the two fixes: I independently re-verified two of the article's load-bearing direct quotes against the live Microsoft Learn pages rather than trusting round 1's transcription -- the PriorityQueue class remarks ('Implements an array-backed, quaternary min-heap ... does not guarantee first-in-first-out semantics for elements of equal priority') and the Remove method's remarks ('The method performs a linear-time scan of every element in the heap, removing the first value found to match the element parameter') both match verbatim. The article's two prerequisite links (breadth-first-and-depth-first-search, heaps-and-priority-queues) both correspond to real rows in CONTENT_PLAN.md, so no dead cross-links. No filler openings or closings, no restated title, no keyword stuffing, no ad code. Structure still doesn't mirror a generic template: it moves proof -> API-driven implementation constraint -> path reconstruction -> two varied exercises -> negative-edge failure mode -> A* generalization, which is a shape distinct from both GeeksforGeeks (language-port catalog) and Wikipedia (abstract theory), and distinct from this pillar's BFS/DFS sibling per the explicit non-overlap the sibling article sets up. `node tools/run-code.mjs` reconfirmed green (16 blocks, 8 executed). I found no new issues in this pass that would justify holding the score below the pass line; the 0.2 short of a higher score reflects that this is a solid, MDN/Real-Python-equal page with only the kind of nits any technical piece this dense could still sharpen (e.g., the A* section's 'letter for letter' claim about Search collapsing to plain Dijkstra at h=0 is true of this article's own code but reads slightly like a general claim about A* implementations -- not worth a formal issue, just a phrase a copyeditor might tighten), not anything AdSense-relevant.
